region/amazon-basin-and-south-american-l.title: Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands
region/amazon-basin-and-south-american-l.summary: The Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands are the forests, river systems, and savannas east of the Andes, home to Indigenous societies whose scale and complexity are being rediscovered through aerial laser survey.
facts: Lidar surveys over the past decade have revealed large networks of earthworks, roads, and settlements beneath the forest; see Casarabe Culture, Upano Valley Settlements, and Xingu Garden Cities.

Indigenous land management, including soil enrichment, shaped much of the forest; see Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths. Scientists dispute whether the dark earths (terra preta) were largely made by people or arose from natural processes that people then used.

European contact after 1492 brought severe population loss from epidemic disease and forced labor. It is debated whether this caused widespread forest regrowth: a 2021 study of 39 fossil pollen records found no synchronized regrowth after European arrival, and found that at most sites land abandonment and regrowth began about 300 to 600 years earlier. The researchers Bush and McMichael argue that populations probably peaked and declined well before 1492. Alexander Koch and colleagues, who proposed the regrowth hypothesis for the Americas as a whole, reply that Amazonia may have been less affected than Mexico, Central America, and the Andes.
The region is the setting of the Marajoara Culture and, at its edges, of many peoples never ruled by the Inca Empire.
region/amazon-basin-and-south-american-l.context: The lowlands sit east of the Andes and were linked to them by trade. They were transformed by the Columbian Exchange.
region/amazon-basin-and-south-american-l.observer: The Observer notes how the phrase 'untouched wilderness' can hide a history of large human societies. What looks like nature can be the product of centuries of deliberate management.
questions: How many people lived in the Amazon before 1500? Published estimates run from about 1 to 2 million up to 8 to 10 million, because little documentation exists and the estimation methods give widely varying results.
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Pre-Columbian Amazon population estimates range from about 1 to 2 million to 8 to 10 million [Wikipedia on Pre-Columbian Amazon Agriculture]
2026-09-20: Dark earths (terra preta) are disputed as to whether they are largely human-made [Wikipedia on Pre-Columbian Amazon Agriculture]

2026-09-25: A 2021 study of 39 fossil pollen records found no synchronous reforestation after European arrival in Amazonia; at most sites land abandonment and forest regrowth began about 300 to 600 years before European arrival (abstract only) [Science 2021 Amazonian Reforestation Pollen Study]

region/andes.title: Andes
region/andes.summary: The Andes are the mountain spine of western South America. Highland and coastal societies developed complex states without wheeled transport or a conventional writing system.
facts: The Inca Empire became the largest pre-Columbian state in the Americas.
Potatoes and llamas were domesticated in the Andes.
The Inca recorded information on knotted cords called quipu.
The site of Machu Picchu dates to the 15th century.
region/andes.context: The Andes were cut off from the Old World until the Columbian Exchange.
region/andes.observer: The Observer notes that the Andes show a state coordinating millions of people using memory-outsourcing that is not writing as most people define it.
questions: What evidence would most change the current picture?

region/arabian-peninsula.title: Arabian Peninsula
region/arabian-peninsula.summary: The Arabian Peninsula is a large, largely arid peninsula between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. It was a corridor for trade and the origin of Islam.
facts: Incense and spice caravans linked southern Arabia with the Mediterranean.
Islam emerged in the Hejaz in the early 7th century; see Rise of Islam and Muhammad.
Monsoon-driven sea trade connected the peninsula with East Africa and South Asia.
region/arabian-peninsula.context: The peninsula sits between Africa and Asia and shaped the growth of the Abbasid Caliphate and later Islamic states.
region/arabian-peninsula.observer: The Observer notes that a sparse region produced a movement that within a century reached from Iberia to Central Asia. Population size and influence are not the same thing.

region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world.title: Caribbean and Atlantic World
region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world.summary: The Caribbean and Atlantic World is the Caribbean basin together with the Atlantic coasts of the Americas, Europe, and Africa that were linked by shipping, trade, and forced migration from the 15th century.
facts: The Caribbean islands were settled by Indigenous peoples, including the Taino and Kalinago, several thousand years before 1492.
Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492; Indigenous populations collapsed within decades through disease, violence, and forced labor.
Sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans made the region among the most valuable in the early modern world.
It was the setting of the Haitian Revolution.
region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world.context: The region is the core arena of the Columbian Exchange and the Atlantic Slave Trade, and of the movements to end slavery; see Abolition of Slavery.
region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world.observer: The Observer sees a zone created by connection: an ocean crossing that turned islands into a hinge between three continents. Its populations, languages, and foods are largely products of that forced mixing.
questions: How large were the pre-contact Indigenous populations?

region/central-asian-oases.title: Central Asian Oases
region/central-asian-oases.summary: The Central Asian Oases are the river valleys and oasis cities between the steppe and the Iranian plateau, including Samarkand and Bukhara, which served as hubs of the Silk Roads.
facts: The region, known in antiquity as Sogdiana and Transoxiana, was home to the Sogdians.
It was conquered by Alexander's Conquests and later brought into the Islamic world in the early 8th century.
It was the center of the Timurid Empire, with its capital at Samarkand.
Scholars such as Ulugh Beg made it a center of astronomy in the 15th century.
region/central-asian-oases.context: The oases lay between the Central Asian Steppe and the Iranian Plateau, and were crossroads of the Opening of the Silk Roads.
region/central-asian-oases.observer: The Observer notes how these cities lived by relaying goods and ideas between larger powers. A place between empires can become an empire of its own kind.
questions: How much did oasis cities shape the ideas that traveled along the Silk Roads?

region/central-asian-steppe.title: Central Asian Steppe
region/central-asian-steppe.summary: The Central Asian Steppe is the vast grassland belt across northern Eurasia. Mounted pastoralists there shaped the history of every neighboring civilization.
facts: Horse domestication and mounted warfare developed on the Western steppe.
The Mongol Empire came from the eastern steppe in the 13th century.
The steppe was a corridor for the Opening of the Silk Roads and for the Indo-European Language Spread.
region/central-asian-steppe.context: The steppe borders East Asia, Europe and the Iranian Plateau; see Genghis Khan.
region/central-asian-steppe.observer: The Observer notes how a mobile way of life without cities repeatedly rearranged the settled world. Absence of monuments is not absence of influence.
questions: What evidence would most change the current picture?

region/east-asia.title: East Asia
region/east-asia.summary: East Asia includes China, Korea, Japan and neighboring regions. China's centralized state tradition is among the longest continuous political traditions.
facts: Farming of millet and rice began independently in the Yellow and Yangtze river basins.
The first unified empire was created in 221 BCE; see Unification of China under Qin.
Major inventions include Paper, Gunpowder, the Magnetic Compass and printing.
Major states included the Shang Dynasty, Han Dynasty and Song Dynasty.
region/east-asia.context: East Asia trades with the Central Asian Steppe and Southeast Asia; see Zheng He and Confucius.
region/east-asia.observer: The Observer notes a distinctive continuity: a written language and administrative tradition that persisted through repeated collapses and re-unifications.
questions: What evidence would most change the current picture?

region/europe.title: Europe
region/europe.summary: Europe is the western peninsula of Eurasia. It hosted early farming societies, the Roman Empire's northern provinces, and later the technologies and empires of the early modern and industrial periods.
facts: Farming spread into Europe from Anatolia over several thousand years.
The Norse traveled from Scandinavia across the Atlantic and through eastern rivers.
The Scientific Revolution and Industrial Revolution began here, drawing on knowledge from many regions.
The continent was the main theater of World War I and World War II.
region/europe.context: Europe links to the Mediterranean Basin and to the Central Asian Steppe. The Movable-Type Printing Press appeared here in the 15th century.
region/europe.observer: The Observer cautions against a common habit: a small peninsula's history is often told as if it were the world's. Its outsized effect in the modern era is real, but recent.
questions: What evidence would most change the current picture?

region/iranian-plateau.title: Iranian Plateau
region/iranian-plateau.summary: The Iranian Plateau is the highland region between Mesopotamia and South Asia. It was the heartland of Persian empires and a link on overland routes across Eurasia.
facts: The Achaemenid Persians built a vast empire from here in the 6th century BCE.
The plateau sits on the routes of the Opening of the Silk Roads.
It was later incorporated into the Abbasid Caliphate and the Mongol Empire.
region/iranian-plateau.context: It links Mesopotamia, South Asia and the Central Asian Steppe.
region/iranian-plateau.observer: The Observer sees the plateau as a hinge region: its historical role was less to originate than to relay, translate, and administer.

region/levant-and-anatolia.title: Levant and Anatolia
region/levant-and-anatolia.summary: The Levant and Anatolia are the eastern Mediterranean coast and the Turkish peninsula. They are a crossroads between Africa, Asia, and Europe and a center of early farming.
facts: Early farming and monumental building appear here, including Göbekli Tepe and Çatalhöyük.
The Phoenicians developed a widely copied alphabet; see Alphabet.
Later, Constantinople stood at the junction of Europe and Asia.
The region saw the collapse of many Bronze Age states; see Bronze Age Collapse.
region/levant-and-anatolia.context: Together with Mesopotamia, this is the core of the Fertile Crescent and of The Agricultural Revolution.
region/levant-and-anatolia.observer: The Observer notes how many meaning-engines share this region as a birthplace or a stage. A dense crossroads seems to produce dense argument about ultimate questions.

region/mediterranean-basin.title: Mediterranean Basin
region/mediterranean-basin.summary: The Mediterranean Basin is the sea and its surrounding coasts. It was one of history's most connected zones of trade, cultural exchange, and conflict.
facts: The sea connects Europe, Africa, and Asia.
Seafaring cultures included the Minoans, Phoenicians, Ancient Greeks and Romans.
Rome eventually ruled the entire coastline; see Rome.
The basin saw both the Bronze Age Collapse and the Fall of the Western Roman Empire.
region/mediterranean-basin.context: The sea served as a highway, and its cities, including Athens and Constantinople, were nodes of exchange.
region/mediterranean-basin.observer: The Observer notes that a shared inland sea acted like a village square for very different peoples, so it generated both intense trade and intense conflict.

region/mesoamerica.title: Mesoamerica
region/mesoamerica.summary: Mesoamerica is the cultural region from central Mexico to Central America. It developed farming (maize, beans, squash), monumental cities, writing, and a sophisticated calendar independently of the Old World.
facts: Early complex societies included the Olmecs.
The Maya developed a full writing system and precise astronomy.
Major cities included Teotihuacan and Tenochtitlan.
The Aztec Empire was conquered by Spain in 1519 to 1521.
region/mesoamerica.context: Mesoamerica was cut off from the Old World until the Columbian Exchange.
region/mesoamerica.observer: The Observer regards Mesoamerica as a natural experiment: a second, independent case of the path from farming to writing, cities and states.
questions: What evidence would most change the current picture?

region/mesopotamia.title: Mesopotamia
region/mesopotamia.summary: Mesopotamia is the land between and around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, in present-day Iraq and parts of neighboring countries. It is a birthplace of cities and writing.
facts: Irrigated farming supported some of the world's first cities, such as Uruk.
Cuneiform writing appeared here about 3400 to 3200 BCE; see Invention of Writing.
Early societies included the Sumerians, later joined by Akkadian, Babylonian and Assyrian states.
The region later became the center of the Abbasid Caliphate.
region/mesopotamia.context: See The Urban Revolution and Hammurabi. Mesopotamia is part of the wider Fertile Crescent, along with the Levant and Anatolia.
region/mesopotamia.observer: The Observer treats Mesopotamia as a laboratory for large-scale coordination: bookkeeping, law, and standardized measurement all appear early here.

region/nile-valley.title: Nile Valley
region/nile-valley.summary: The Nile Valley is the narrow, fertile corridor of the Nile River through northeastern Africa, home to one of the earliest states.
facts: The Nile floods annually, depositing silt that supported dense farming in a desert setting.
Egypt was unified about 3100 BCE; see Unification of Egypt.
Nile Valley peoples included the Ancient Egyptians and, to the south, Nubian kingdoms.
Monuments such as Giza Necropolis date from the third millennium BCE.
region/nile-valley.context: The valley links Africa with the Mediterranean and the Levant, and it was an early center of administrative writing.
region/nile-valley.observer: The Observer sees the Nile as a natural clock: predictable flooding produced predictable calendars, and predictable calendars supported large, centralized states.

region/north-america.title: North America
region/north-america.summary: North America north of Mexico was settled by peoples who arrived at least 15,000 years ago and who developed diverse societies, from mobile hunters to farming towns and confederacies.
facts: The Peopling of the Americas began during the last ice age.
Regional societies included the mound-building cultures of the Mississippi valley and Ancestral Puebloans.
The Haudenosaunee Confederacy was a political union of five (later six) nations.
European colonization from the 16th century changed the continent through disease and conquest.
region/north-america.context: The region is closely tied to the Columbian Exchange and to the Age of Revolutions.
region/north-america.observer: The Observer notes a wide range of political forms that did not resemble the states of the Old World, and that are easy to overlook if 'civilization' is defined by cities and writing.

region/oceania.title: Oceania
region/oceania.summary: Oceania includes Australia, New Guinea, and the Pacific islands. It holds both the oldest continuing cultures outside Africa and the last large landmasses settled by humans.

New Guinea was an independent center of agriculture.
Polynesian navigators settled the remote Pacific; see Polynesians and Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific.
Aotearoa New Zealand was among the last habitable lands settled, around 1250 to 1300 CE.
region/oceania.context: Oceania sits at the edge of Southeast Asia and the wider Pacific.
region/oceania.observer: The Observer regards Oceania as home to the species' most spectacular feats of navigation and its longest continuous cultural traditions.

region/planet-wide.title: Planet-wide
region/planet-wide.summary: Planet-wide is the region tag for events and processes that affect the whole Earth, or that have no single location, such as mass extinctions, climate shifts, and global exchange networks.

Earth's surface is about 510 million square kilometers, of which about 71 percent is ocean.

region/planet-wide.observer: The Observer treats the planet as the primary unit of analysis, and human regions as subdivisions of a single connected system. Regional labels are useful bookkeeping, not natural divisions.

region/siberia-and-the-arctic.title: Siberia and the Arctic
region/siberia-and-the-arctic.summary: Siberia and the Arctic are the northern lands of Asia from the Urals to the Pacific, and the Arctic coasts beyond, where cold and permafrost shaped both human ways of life and the preservation of the past.
facts: Some of the oldest known human genomes come from Siberia; see Mal'ta and the Ancient North Eurasians.
Permafrost and ice preserved frozen tombs of the Scythians in the Altai.
The Yakut (Sakha), Evenki, Chukchi, and many other peoples developed herding, hunting, and fishing economies; see Yakut (Sakha).
Russia expanded across Siberia to the Pacific between 1582 and 1639; see Russian Expansion into Siberia.
region/siberia-and-the-arctic.context: Siberia borders the Central Asian Steppe and East Asia, and was linked to North America by Beringia during the Last Glacial Maximum.
region/siberia-and-the-arctic.observer: The Observer notes that the coldest lands of the planet hold some of the best records of the species' past, since cold preserves what warmth destroys.

region/sub-saharan-africa.title: Sub-Saharan Africa
region/sub-saharan-africa.summary: Sub-Saharan Africa is the region south of the Sahara. It is the birthplace of the hominin lineage and of Homo sapiens, and it holds the greatest human genetic and linguistic diversity.

The Bantu Expansion spread Bantu languages across much of central, eastern and southern Africa.

Trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean trade linked the region to Eurasia; see Timbuktu.

region/sub-saharan-africa.observer: The Observer notes that the species' longest history happened here. Every non-African population is, in genetic terms, a subset of African diversity.
